segments.translit: maitrīmayaḥ sarahapādas tam evārthaṃ kāyanaukāvyājena pratipādayati—
segments.translation: [Saraha]{p-saraha}, full of [loving-kindness]{maitri}, sets forth that very meaning under the guise of the [body]{body} as a [boat]{boat}:
segments.note: Munidatta says that [Saraha]{p-saraha}, full of [loving-kindness]{maitri}, sets forth that same meaning under the guise of the [body]{body} as a [boat]{boat} (cp.38.m1). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads lus la glu, 'the body as a song', probably a slip for gru, 'boat', and renders 'guise' as dgongs pa'i skad, 'intentional language'.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has byams pa'i rang bzhin can sa ra ha'i zhabs kyis kyang don de nyid lus la glu dgongs pa'i skad kyis gsungs so. Its glu, 'song', is probably a slip for gru, 'boat' (the two differ only in the subscript, l for r), answering Munidatta's kāyanaukā, 'body-boat' (cp.38.m1). It renders vyājena, 'under the guise of', with dgongs pa'i skad kyis, 'in intentional language', its usual term for sandhyā-bhāṣā, and adds kyang, 'Saraha too'. The translation follows the Sanskrit, so vyāja is not linked to the twilight-language entry.

tam evārthaṃ, 'that very meaning', has no antecedent inside this comment (cp.38.m1): Munidatta seems to tie song 38 to the song before it, and the Tibetan's kyang, 'too', points the same way. He does not restate that meaning here, so the note does not name it.

segments.translit:
kāa nābaṛī khaṇṭītyādi| ādhārādheyasambandhena kāya[ṃ] naukā[ṃ] parikalpya manovijñāna[ṃ] kelipātañ ca| satguruvaca[naṃ] patabāla[ṃ] gṛhītvā| vajrajalajasaṃyogabhavajaladhimadhye pañcajñānātmakaṃ vilakṣaṇaśodhitasaṃvṛtibodhicittaṃ sthirīkṛtya kāyanaurakṣāṃ kuru bho sarahapāda| bhavasamudraṃ tarttuṃ nānyopāyo vidyate|
tathā ca iuṛīpādānāṃ|
ete pañca yaṃti mohataṭinīpāram ityādi|
segments.translation:
'The [body]{body} is a sound little [boat]{boat}…' and so on. Having imagined, through the relation of [support and supported]{adhara-adheya}, the [body]{body} as the [boat]{boat} and mind-[consciousness]{vijnana} as the [oar]{keruala}; having taken the true [guru]{guru}'s word as the [patabāla]{patabala}; and having made [steady]{sthira}, in the middle of the [ocean]{ocean} of [existence]{bhava}, through the union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}, the [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} that has the nature of the [five wisdoms]{pancajnana} and is purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana}: guard the [body]{body}-[boat]{boat}, O [Saraha]{p-saraha}! To cross the [ocean]{ocean} of [existence]{bhava} there is no other [means]{upaya}.
And so, in the words of [Iuṛīpāda]{p-iuri}:
'These five go to the [far shore]{para} of the [river]{river} of [delusion]{moha},' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta frames the body-boat through [support and supported]{adhara-adheya}: body as [boat]{boat}, mind-consciousness as [oar]{keruala}, the true [guru]{guru}'s word as the [patabāla]{patabala}, which he leaves unexplained, deciding neither helm nor sail. Where 2a steadies the mind he puts [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}; for 'hold it, boatman' he has 'guard the body-boat, O Saraha' (cp.38.m2). No other [means]{upaya} crosses existence's [ocean]{ocean}.

equations.en: the body, imagined as the boat through the relation of support and supported
the true guru's word, set in apposition ('having taken the true guru's word as the patabāla'), not explained

citations.quoted: These five go to the far shore of the river of delusion
citations.work: a verse of Iuṛīpāda, as Munidatta names him (work not named; the Tibetan has u Da'i zhabs)

flags.note: patabāla: Munidatta (cp.38.m2) keeps the word (patavāla) in source form and sets it in apposition to the true guru's word, 'having taken the true guru's word as the patabāla', so the song's 'with the true guru's word, hold the patabāla' becomes an identification. He says nothing of the object itself; gṛhītvā, 'having grasped', suits a helm or steering oar at least as well as a sail. The Tibetan points to steering: its line 1b has skya ba 'dzin pa, 'holding the oar'; its comment here has 'having seized it with the mnyen pa (sense uncertain) of the true guru's speech'; and its comment on the next couplet renders karṇadhāra, 'helm-holder, helmsman', as skya ba 'dzin pa ('oar-holder'), the very phrase of its line 1b (cp.38.m3). Neither witness suggests a sail.

নাহী (2a): Munidatta (cp.38.m2) does not gloss it. His paraphrase of the refrain, 'having made conventional bodhicitta steady, guard the body-boat, O Sarahapāda', supplies both a boat to be guarded and an addressee, so it fits either 'boat' (nāhī for nāvī, the object of dhahu, with re rendered by bho) or 'boatman' (re nāhī as the vocative, which he turns into Saraha). It gives no support to the negative (nāhi, 'not'): his 'there is no other means' renders the ṇa of 2b. The Tibetan line has gru pa rnams, 'boatmen', which supports the draft; the Tibetan comment's vocative, kye'i sa ra ha'i zhabs, opens the next sentence instead.

Where Munidatta has kāyanaurakṣāṃ kuru, 'guard the body-boat' (cp.38.m2), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lus kyi gru mi 'gyur bar gyis shig, 'make the body's boat unchanging'; mi 'gyur ba usually renders akṣara, 'imperishable', so the translators either rendered rakṣā loosely or divided the compound otherwise. It has the true guru's speech as the instrument ('seized with the mnyen pa of the true guru's speech'), closer to the song than the Sanskrit apposition, and the union of vajra and lotus as instrument too (mnyam par sbyor bas). In the Iuṛīpāda verse it has 'these five ferry across (sgrol bar byed) from the bank ('gram) of delusion / to the far shore…': transitive for yaṃti, 'go', bank for taṭinī, 'river', and a second line the Sanskrit cuts off.

vajrajalajasaṃyogabhavajaladhimadhye (cp.38.m2) can be divided as 'in the middle of the ocean of existence, (in or through) the union of vajra and lotus' (taken, with the Tibetan rdo rje dang chu skyes mnyam par sbyor bas srid pa'i chu gter gyi dbus su) or as 'in the middle of the ocean born of (-bhava) the union of vajra and lotus'. Munidatta's own bhavasamudraṃ in the next sentence favours 'ocean of existence'.

Munidatta (cp.38.m2) names the relation of support and supported but does not say what the body-boat supports; the Tibetan (rten dang brten pa'i 'brel bas) is equally bare, and the note adds nothing. He also does not say who 'these five' are in the Iuṛīpāda verse, which follows his mention of the five wisdoms; the identification is left open.

Shastri's restorations kāya[ṃ], naukā[ṃ], manovijñāna[ṃ], satguruvaca[naṃ] and patabāla[ṃ] supply the accusative endings and are translated through. The lemma is spelled nāvaṛī khaṇṭī against the song's ṇābaṛi khāṇṭi; Munidatta does not gloss khāṇṭi (cp.38.m2) ('sound'), and the Tibetan line and lemma have gru'i dum bu, 'a piece of a boat'.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena mārgasyānuśaṃsām āha—
nobāa ityādi yathā bāhye naukāṃ vāhayati karṇadhāra[ḥ] guṇenākarṣayati ca tadvad iyaṃ naur na bhavati| bho yogin vajragurau sahajānandopāyaṃ gṛhītvā nauparityāgaṃ kuru| sadya[ḥ] yena mahāsukhadvīpaṃ gaccha|
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga}:
'The [boatman]{boatman}…' and so on. As, outwardly, a [helmsman]{helmsman} drives a [boat]{boat} and hauls it by the [towrope]{guna-towrope}, this [boat]{boat} is not like that. O [yogi]{yogi}, having taken from the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru} the [means]{upaya} of [innate joy]{sahajananda}, give up the [boat]{boat}; by that means go at once to the [island]{island} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga} (cp.38.m3). This boat is not like an outer one, driven by a [helmsman]{helmsman} and hauled by a [towrope]{guna-towrope}: having taken the means of [innate joy]{sahajananda} from the vajra guru, the [yogi]{yogi} should give it up and so go at once to the [island]{island} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. The Tibetan reverses this.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reverses two of Munidatta's statements (cp.38.m3). For tadvad iyaṃ naur na bhavati, 'this boat is not like that', it has de bzhin du 'dir gru ni yang nyams su myong ba'o, 'likewise here too the boat is to be experienced'; nyams su myong ba is the usual rendering of anubhava, so its exemplar may have read naur anubhavati (নৌরনুভবতি) for naur na bhavati (নৌর্ন ভবতি), a difference of a stroke or two. For nauparityāgaṃ kuru, 'give up the boat', it has gru ni yongs su ma spong cig, 'do not abandon the boat'. The Tibetan readings hang together, as does its line 3b, which takes meli mela as tshogs, 'gathering', not 'letting go'. The translation follows the Sanskrit.

Munidatta's simile, a helmsman who 'drives the boat and hauls it by the guṇa' (guṇenākarṣayati, cp.38.m3), makes the guṇa the hauling line and supports the draft's 'towrope' in 3a; his vāhayati and ākarṣayati also echo the song's naubāhī and ṭāgua. The Tibetan reads guṇa as yon tan, 'quality': its comment has the boat's going drawn 'by the quality of the oar-holder' (skya ba 'dzin pa'i yon tan gyis), and its line 3a has 'it is the quality (yon tan) of the boat-timber's mnyen pa'. Its skya ba 'dzin pa renders karṇadhāra, 'helmsman', and is the phrase of its line 1b.

yena, masculine or neuter, cannot refer to the feminine nau, 'boat'; it picks up upāya, 'the means' (cp.38.m3): the yogin reaches the island by the means of innate joy once the boat is given up. The Tibetan's gang gi, 'by which', coming after its 'do not abandon the boat', reads naturally as the boat.

Munidatta cites the line as নোবাঅ (nobāa) for the song's naubāhī (cp.38.m3); the Tibetan cites gru ni 'bab dang, 'the boat flows down and…', following its own line 3a. Where the song has a boatman (naubāhī), his simile has a helmsman (karṇadhāra). The folio number in gṛhī[৫৫ক]tvā and Shastri's restorations karṇadhāra[ḥ] and sadya[ḥ] are translated through.

vajragurau is locative, literally 'in the vajra guru' (cp.38.m3); rendered 'from the vajra guru', as the source of the means. The Tibetan has the genitive, rdo rje bla ma'i, 'the vajra guru's means of innate joy'.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena mārakarmādhiṣṭhānam āha—
bāṭata ityādi| khānapānaviṣayāśaktitvena sādhako yadā mārgabhraṣṭo bhavati, avadhūtīṃ gatvā jahā(ha)tīti| khaṇṭam iti tadā candrasūryau dvau balavantau bhavataḥ tena hetunā bhavasamudraviṣayollālanena nairātmyadharmasarvaprakāreṇa bolitam iti|
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks of the sway of [Māra]{mara}'s work:
'On the [road]{road}…' and so on. When the practitioner, through attachment to food, drink and [sense objects]{visaya}, falls from the [path]{marga}, having gone to the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} he abandons it. 'Block' (khaṇṭa) means: then the two, the [moon]{moon} and the [sun]{surya}, become strong. For that reason, through the surging of the [sense objects]{visaya} in the [ocean]{ocean} of [existence]{bhava}, the [dharma]{dharma} of [selflessness]{nairatmya} is sunk in every way.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as the sway of [Māra]{mara}'s work (cp.38.m4). Attached to food, drink and [sense objects]{visaya}, the practitioner falls from the [path]{marga}, having gone to the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} and abandoned it; the strong who block are the [moon]{moon} and the [sun]{surya}, grown strong; and through the surging sense objects of existence's [ocean]{ocean} the [dharma]{dharma} of [selflessness]{nairatmya} is sunk.

equations.src: খণ্ট khaṇṭa (the song's খাণ্টবি বলআ khāṇṭabi balaā)
equations.en: then the two, the moon and the sun, become strong (balavantau)

flags.note: khānapānaviṣayāśaktitvena (cp.38.m4) is written with শ, but the word is āsakti, 'attachment' (ā-sakti, from sañj, 'cling'), not śakti, 'power': 'through attachment to food, drink and sense objects'. The Tibetan confirms it with chags pa, 'attached'. It is therefore not linked to the śakti entry; see questions.

mārakarmādhiṣṭhānam (cp.38.m4): adhiṣṭhāna here is the seat, hold or sway of Māra's work, not 'blessing', the sense of the adhisthana entry, so it is rendered 'sway' and left unlinked. The Tibetan has bdud kyi las su gnas pa, 'abiding in Māra's work'. Likewise tena hetunā is the idiom 'for that reason' and is not linked to the hetu entry.

avadhūtīṃ gatvā jahā(ha)tīti (cp.38.m4) is obscure. Shastri's '(ha)' marks a doubtful syllable; the verb is jahāti, 'leaves, abandons', its object unstated (most naturally the avadhūtī). Munidatta's yadā, 'when', seems to find its tadā, 'then', only after khaṇṭam iti, so the sense may run 'when he falls from the path… then the moon and the sun grow strong'. The Tibetan has a wa d+hU tIr song bas spang ba'i phyir ro, 'because, having gone to the avadhūtī, it is abandoned', agreeing on 'abandon'.

bolitam (cp.38.m4) Sanskritizes the song's boliā; Sanskrit bul/bolayati, 'submerge', supports 'sunk'. The Tibetan comment has 'khrul par gyur pa, 'became confused', and its line 4b has rnam par 'khrugs par gyur, 'were thrown into turmoil'. Its lemma for khaṇṭa is 'gog pa, 'blocking', agreeing with the draft's 'block'; its rab tu byed pas looks like a calque of prakāreṇa.

nairātmyadharmasarvaprakāreṇa bolitam (cp.38.m4) fuses 'the dharma of selflessness' into the instrumental 'in every way'; read as nairātmyadharmaḥ sarvaprakāreṇa bolitaḥ, 'the dharma of selflessness is sunk in every way', where the song has 'everything (ṣaa) is sunk'. The Tibetan likewise separates bdag med pa'i chos la, 'with regard to the dharma of selflessness'.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena avadhūtīmārgasyānuśaṃsām āha—
kulala ityādi kulam iti| kumārgacandrādikaṃ yasminn avadhūtyāṃ layaṃ gacchati sā pra[kṛ]tipariśuddhā avadhūtikā ku[la?]śabdena boddhavyā| laa iti tāṃ gṛhītvā kharasontem iti mahāsukharāgasrotāvartena paramārthavidāṃ yo bodhicittavajraḥ sa ūrdhvaṃ gacchati| gaganeti vaimalyacakradvīpe antarbhavati| 38|
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga} of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}:
'Keeping to the [shore]{kula-shore}…' and so on. '[Shore]{kula-shore}' (kula): the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} in which the bad path (kumārga), the [moon]{moon} and the rest, goes to dissolution (laya), that [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, purified by nature, is to be understood by the word kula. 'Taking' (laa) means: having taken her. 'In the strong [current]{current}' means: through the whirl of the stream of the [passion]{raga-passion} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, the [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}-[vajra]{vajra} of those who know the [ultimate]{paramartha} goes upward. 'In the [sky]{gagana}' means: it comes to be within the [island]{island} of the stainless wheel.
segments.note: Munidatta derives kula, '[shore]{kula-shore}', from ku, the bad path of the [moon]{moon} and the rest, and la, its dissolution (laya): the naturally pure [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, which is taken. Through the whirling stream of great bliss's passion the [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}-vajra goes upward, and 'in the [sky]{gagana}' means it comes within the [island]{island} of the stainless wheel (cp.38.m5).

equations.en: the avadhūtī, purified by nature, in which the bad path (ku-mārga), the moon and the rest, goes to dissolution (la-ya)
the whirl of the stream of the passion of great bliss, by which the bodhicitta-vajra of those who know the ultimate goes upward
in the island of the stainless wheel (vaimalyacakra), within which it comes to be

flags.note: Munidatta has the bodhicitta-vajra go upward (ūrdhvaṃ gacchati) in the strong current (cp.38.m5), as the draft's 5a 'goes upstream' (ujāa) does. The Tibetan line reads the opposite: pha rol tshu rol chu rgyun drag po rab tu 'bab, 'far shore, near shore, the strong current flows down hard', with 'both banks' for kula. The Tibetan comment, however, agrees with Munidatta: de steng du 'gro bar byed do, 'it goes upward'. So the Tibetan line and its own comment disagree here.

antarbhavati (cp.38.m5), Munidatta's word where the song has pamāe, means 'comes to be within, is contained in': the bodhicitta-vajra passes into the island of the stainless wheel. It supports the draft's 5b 'absorbed in the sky' only in the sense of being taken into, merging, not of rapt meditation; the Tibetan comment agrees, with thim par 'gyur, 'dissolves into'. The Tibetan line has nam mkha'i ting nge 'dzin, 'sky-samādhi', a noun for meditative absorption, perhaps from a reading samāe or samāhi for pamāe. English 'absorbed' carries both senses.

ku[la?]śabdena (cp.38.m5): the '-la' is Shastri's doubtful restoration. 'By the word kula' fits Munidatta's derivation (ku from kumārga, la from laya), but the Tibetan has a wa d+hU tI'i sgras rtogs par bya, 'to be understood by the word avadhūtī', so it does not confirm the restoration. The Tibetan lemma kun la is probably a garbled ku la; it renders the derivation's laya with thim pa, 'dissolve'.

Munidatta glosses laa as tāṃ gṛhītvā, 'having taken her' (cp.38.m5), so he reads 5a as 'taking the shore', where the draft has 'keeping to the shore'. The lemma is translated with the draft's words; 'taking' is used for laa in the gloss. The Tibetan transliterates la ya and glosses de gzung nas, 'having seized it'.

In cp.38.m5, yasmin (masculine) stands with the feminine avadhūtyāṃ; kharasontemeti is read kharasontem iti; srotāvarta is taken as srotas-āvarta, 'the whirl of the stream'. The Tibetan has rgyun gyis 'jug pas, 'entering by the stream', and don dam pa rig pa, 'the knower of the ultimate', in the singular. The closing '38' is the song number and is not translated.
vaimalyacakra, 'the stainless wheel' (Tibetan dri ma med pa'i 'khor lo), is not otherwise named in the commentary (cp.38.m5); it is rendered literally and left unlinked.

questions: patabāla (1b): Munidatta keeps the word and only sets it beside the true guru's word (cp.38.m2). The Tibetan points to steering: skya ba 'oar' in line 1b, and skya ba 'dzin pa for karṇadhāra 'helmsman' in its comment on couplet 3 (cp.38.m3). Nothing suggests a sail. Keep the source form, or render 'helm'?

নাহী (2a): Munidatta's 'guard the body-boat, O Sarahapāda' (cp.38.m2) fits either 'boat' or the vocative 'boatman', and nothing supports the negative. The Tibetan line's gru pa rnams 'boatmen' backs the draft. Keep 'boatman'?

5b 'absorbed in the sky': Munidatta's antarbhavati, 'comes to be within' (cp.38.m5), and the Tibetan comment's thim par 'gyur mean being taken into, merging. The Tibetan line's nam mkha'i ting nge 'dzin is meditative absorption (samādhi). 'Absorbed' covers both. Would 'merges into the sky' or 'enters the sky' be closer to the song, or is the ambiguity worth keeping?
5a 'Keeping to the shore': Munidatta glosses laa as 'having taken her' (cp.38.m5), and lai is literally 'taking'. Consider 'Taking the shore'?

m3: the Sanskrit tells the yogin to give up the boat, and the Tibetan tells him not to (cp.38.m3). I have translated the Sanskrit, given the Tibetan in a flag, and closed the woven note with 'The Tibetan reverses this.' Is that enough, or should the note leave the Tibetan out?
āsakti in khānapānaviṣayāśaktitvena (cp.38.m4) is left unlinked. Should it become a form of the abhisvanga entry (also 'attachment'), or get its own entry? It must not match the śakti entry.

adhiṣṭhāna in mārakarmādhiṣṭhāna (cp.38.m4) means sway or seat, not the adhisthana entry's 'blessing'. I left it unlinked and rendered it 'sway'. Add a second sense to the entry, or keep the two apart? hetu in the idiom tena hetunā is also left unlinked.
p-saraha: Munidatta always says Sarahapāda (cp.38.m1, cp.38.m2), but the entry lists no variant, so I wrote [Saraha]. Add 'Sarahapāda' as a variant?
vaimalyacakra, 'the stainless wheel' (cp.38.m5), has no entry and is not identified elsewhere. Propose an entry, or leave it as plain words?
